speaker: Student Notes
content: Key Concepts: Refraction, Reflection, and Distortions in Glass

speaker: Student Notes
content: 1. Refraction and Snell's Law

speaker: Student Notes
content: When light passes through a window, it enters the glass (bending inward) and then exits back into the air (correcting outward). Because the process is symmetric, the light exits traveling in the same direction it started, making the window resilient to surface imperfections and thickness variations.

speaker: Student Notes
content: 2. Reflection vs. Transmission

speaker: Student Notes
content: Unlike light passing through glass, reflections only bounce off a single surface. Consequently, they lack the corrective effect of exiting through a second surface. A minor, one-degree deflection in the glass causes a two-degree change in the apparent position of a reflected object (like a tree or the sun), which leads to the visible wobbling.

speaker: Student Notes
content: 3. The Paradox Solved

speaker: Student Notes
content: During the day, people looking from the inside are viewing transmitted light (clear), while those on the outside are primarily viewing distorted reflections. At night, this relationship flips as indoor lighting makes reflections more dominant from the inside.
